title: Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of ostrich and emu farming

lessons.title: Ostriches and emus: differences and commercial value
lessons.html:
Two ratites

Ostriches and emus are ratites: large, flightless birds with a flat breastbone. They are often farmed for similar products, but they are different species with different biology, behaviour and management needs.

FeatureOstrich (Struthio camelus)Emu (Dromaius novaehollandiae)
OriginAfricaAustralia
SizeThe largest living bird; adults commonly well over 2 m tallSmaller; adults roughly up to about 1.9 m
ToesTwo toes, one with a large clawThree toes
PlumageMales black and white; females grey-brown; bare neck and thighsShaggy grey-brown feathers on both sexes; double-shafted feathers
EggsCream-white, very largeDark green, smaller
Incubation in natureBoth parents share incubationThe male incubates and raises the chicks
KickForward and down with great forceSideways and backwards

Commercial value

South Africa has one of the world's largest commercial ostrich industries, centred historically on Oudtshoorn in the Klein Karoo and spread through the Western and Eastern Cape. Products include:

  • Leather - the characteristic quill-follicle pattern makes it a high-value luxury leather.
  • Meat - a red meat that is low in fat, sold locally and exported.
  • Feathers - for fashion, décor and feather dusters.
  • Other - eggshells for crafts, live-bird tourism.

Emus are farmed on a much smaller scale, mainly for emu oil (from fat, used in cosmetics and health products), meat and leather. Emu farming in South Africa is a niche activity, and markets are small and less established.

Economics

Ostrich profitability is strongly affected by export market access. Outbreaks of avian influenza have repeatedly closed export markets for ostrich meat, which shows how important disease control and biosecurity are to the industry's value. Farmers should assess market access, abattoir availability, feed costs and capital costs before investing.

lessons.title: Requirements: nutrition, water, health, housing, behaviour and welfare
lessons.html:
General requirements

Nutrition

  • Both species are mainly herbivores with a large hindgut that ferments fibre; ostriches in particular use fibre efficiently.
  • Ostriches in South Africa are commonly raised on lucerne pastures supplemented with balanced rations; emus need a balanced ratite ration plus forage.
  • Rations differ by age: high-quality, lower-fibre starter feeds for chicks; grower and finisher rations; maintenance and breeder rations. Use rations formulated for ratites by a qualified nutritionist and registered feeds.
  • Birds swallow grit and stones, and also swallow foreign objects such as wire, nails and plastic, which can cause fatal impaction. Keep camps clean.

Water

Clean, fresh water must always be available, in troughs the birds can reach and that chicks cannot drown in. Water intake rises sharply in heat. Check troughs daily.

Health

  • Common problems: chick mortality from poor hygiene, temperature stress and infections; impaction; leg problems in fast-growing chicks; parasites; injuries from fences and fighting.
  • Avian influenza and Newcastle disease are of major concern. Report suspected outbreaks to the state veterinarian as the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 requires.
  • Work with a veterinarian on a health and biosecurity plan: footbaths, controlled visitor access, keeping wild birds away from feed and water, quarantine for new birds.

Housing

  • Camps with strong, high, smooth fencing; no barbed wire. Fences must be clearly visible because birds running in panic may hit them.
  • Shelter from extreme heat, cold and rain, especially for chicks and young birds.
  • Well-drained ground; avoid mud and sharp debris.
  • Adequate space to run; overcrowding increases fighting and stress.

Behaviour and welfare

Ostriches are flock birds, easily startled, and can panic and injure themselves. Breeding males become aggressive and territorial. Emus are curious, more docile in general, but can also kick and are strong. Welfare is based on the Five Freedoms: freedom from hunger and thirst, discomfort, pain, injury and disease, freedom to express normal behaviour, and freedom from fear and distress. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies to farmed ratites as to other animals.

lessons.title: Handling, legislation and stages of development
lessons.html:
Handling

Both species can seriously injure people. An ostrich kicks forward and downward with a large claw that can cause deep wounds; a breeding male in a camp is particularly dangerous.

  • Plan handling, use enough trained people, and work quietly and slowly.
  • Never stand directly in front of an ostrich. Approach from the side or behind.
  • Use a hooking stick (crook) on the neck to lower the head of an ostrich, then place a hood over the head. A hooded bird usually becomes calm and can be guided by holding the wings and tail feathers from behind and the side.
  • If threatened by an ostrich with no escape, lie flat on the ground face down and protect your head, because the bird cannot kick downward effectively at a flat person; or hold a thorn branch or stick high in front of you.
  • Emus are handled from behind or the side, with one arm over the back and the bird held against the handler's body, keeping clear of the feet.
  • Chicks are lifted with a hand under the body, supporting the legs; never lift by the neck or legs alone.

Legislation, standards and codes

  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 - welfare, cruelty offences.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 - controlled and notifiable diseases such as avian influenza; movement controls and veterinary procedures. Ostrich farms are subject to state veterinary registration and movement control requirements; consult the state vet.
  • Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 - slaughter at registered abattoirs and meat hygiene.
  • Act 36 of 1947 - registration of farm feeds and stock remedies.
  • Industry codes of practice and welfare guidelines for ostrich farming, and export requirements for meat and leather.
  • Provincial nature conservation legislation may apply to keeping or moving emus as an exotic species; check with the provincial authority.

Development stages

StageHousingFeedingWelfare focus
Hatchling (first days)Warm, clean brooder; non-slip floorRelies on the yolk sac at first; then starter feed and waterTemperature, hygiene, prevent leg splaying
Chick (first months)Brooder with access to sunny outdoor run; protection from cold and rainHigh-quality starter ration, fresh greens, gritHighest mortality period; avoid stress and overcrowding
GrowerLarger camps with shelterGrower ration, lucerne pastureLeg problems, impaction, injuries
Slaughter birdFeedlot or campsFinisher rationLow stress before slaughter to protect welfare and meat and skin quality
BreederBreeding camps, pairs or triosBreeder ration with correct mineralsAggression in males, injuries

lessons.title: Breeders, eggs, incubation, capture and transport
lessons.html:
Breeder birds

  • Select breeders for good health, conformation, temperament, and records of fertility, egg production and chick survival.
  • Ostriches are often kept as breeding pairs or trios (one male with two females) in separate breeding camps. Breeding males show red colouring on the beak and shins in the breeding season and become aggressive.
  • Emus form pairs; the male takes over the nest and incubates.
  • Feed a breeder ration before and during the season, with correct calcium for eggshell formation.

Egg collection

  1. Collect eggs at least daily, using two people in ostrich camps: one to distract or guard against the male.
  2. Wear clean gloves; mark each egg with the camp, female (if known) and date.
  3. Do not wash eggs with water; clean dirty eggs by dry brushing and sanitise following the hatchery's procedure.
  4. Store in a cool, clean room, pointed end down or as the hatchery specifies, and turn them regularly. Set them in the incubator within the storage period the hatchery allows.

Incubation

  • Commercial operations use artificial incubators with controlled temperature, humidity, turning and ventilation, set to manufacturer and specialist recommendations for each species.
  • Ostrich eggs take about 42 days to hatch; emu eggs take longer, roughly 7 to 8 weeks.
  • Candle eggs at set times to remove infertile eggs and dead embryos.
  • Move eggs to the hatcher shortly before hatching. Record weight loss, fertility and hatch rates for every breeding group.
  • Strict hygiene in the hatchery is essential.

Capture, transport and release

  • Capture: move birds calmly into a narrowing funnel or pen with high, solid, smooth sides. Avoid chasing; panicked birds break legs and necks. Hood adult ostriches before loading. Capture in cool parts of the day.
  • Transport: use vehicles with high sides, non-slip floors, adequate ventilation and partitions; separate birds by size; do not overcrowd; avoid sudden braking. Chicks travel in ventilated, clean boxes with temperature control. Ensure any required veterinary movement documents are in place before moving birds.
  • Release: unload quietly into a prepared camp with water, feed and visible fencing; remove hoods once birds are in the camp; observe them for injuries and settling over the following days.

Key points

  • Ostriches (Africa, two toes) and emus (Australia, three toes) differ in biology, behaviour and products.
  • Ostrich leather, low-fat meat and feathers are valuable, but market access depends on disease control.
  • Provide clean water, ratite rations, strong visible fencing and clean camps free of wire and plastic.
  • Never stand in front of an ostrich; use a crook and hood and enough trained handlers.
  • Collect eggs daily, store and incubate under strict hygiene, and capture and transport birds calmly with legal documents.
